c.tagline: Alpine city of Zenko-ji pilgrims, 1998 Olympic legacy, and gateway to the Japanese Alps.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered with a base fare around ¥700-800 (~$4-5); readily available at Nagano Station taxi stands, though less common to hail on the street outside downtown.

emergency.note: Japan has no single unified emergency number; 110 reaches police and 119 reaches fire and ambulance services.

hood_desc: The modern hub around JR/Shinkansen Nagano Station with department stores, chain hotels, and the Zenkoji-guchi exit leading straight toward the temple; best for travelers prioritizing easy Shinkansen access and reliable business hotels.

The atmospheric pilgrim approach to Zenko-ji, one of Japan's most important Buddhist temples, lined with the Nakamise shopping street's traditional shops, soba restaurants, and temple lodgings; suits travelers who want to be steps from the city's spiritual heart.

Nagano's historic covered shopping arcade and downtown core linking the station to Zenko-ji, packed with local eateries, izakaya, and everyday shops; good for travelers who want a walkable, lived-in city-center base.

A preserved former castle town on the city's edge with samurai residences, earthen storehouses, and the ruins of Matsushiro Castle; suits travelers seeking a quieter, history-focused stay away from the station bustle.

A mountain district on Nagano's western fringe centered on the ancient Togakushi Shrine complex and cedar-lined pilgrim trails; suits nature lovers and hikers wanting an alpine, forested base near the Japanese Alps.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink everywhere.

transit.hours: Trains and buses generally run about 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM; no late-night service.
transit.pay: IC cards (Suica/ICOCA compatible) are widely accepted on trains and most city buses; cash also works on buses.
transit.note: The Hokuriku Shinkansen makes Nagano an easy ~80-minute trip from Tokyo; local Nagaden trains and Alpico buses connect the station to Zenko-ji and outlying areas like Togakushi and the Snow Monkey Park.

air: Shinshu Matsumoto Airport (regional; most visitors arrive via Tokyo by Shinkansen)
bus: Highway buses to Tokyo, Matsumoto, and Kanazawa

airport.name: Shinshu Matsumoto Airport (FDA) — most visitors instead arrive via Hokuriku Shinkansen from Tokyo (~80 min)

transit.m: Airport bus to Matsumoto then train to Nagano (~90 min total)
Hokuriku Shinkansen from Tokyo Station (~80 min, unrelated to this airport)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in Japan and can even cause confusion; excellent service is simply the standard, not something to reward with extra cash.

food.name: Togakushi soba
food.desc: Buckwheat noodles from the mountain village above the city, served cold in bocchi mori bundles on a woven basket.

places.name: Uzuraya
places.note: Beside the Chusha shrine gate and consistently the most sought-after soba here.

places.name: Yamaguchiya
places.note: Long-established Togakushi shop, less queueing than Uzuraya.

places.name: Daimaru
places.note: Old soba house on the temple approach, open since the Edo period.

food.name: Oyaki
food.desc: Buckwheat-flour dumplings stuffed with nozawana greens, aubergine or pumpkin, then steamed or seared on an iron plate.

places.name: Ogawa no Sho
places.note: The best-known oyaki maker, with a hearth-grilled version.

places.name: Irohado
places.note: Handmade oyaki to eat on the temple approach.

places.name: Nishinomon Yoshinoya
places.note: Oyaki and Shinshu dishes in a converted merchant house.

food.name: Basashi
food.desc: Raw horse meat sliced thin and eaten with ginger, garlic and sweet soy - a Nagano izakaya staple, not a novelty.

places.name: Gondo shopping arcade izakaya
places.note: Covered arcade lined with izakaya that all carry basashi.

places.name: Zenkoji Omotesando izakaya
places.note: Evening spots on the temple approach serving Shinshu specialities.

places.name: MIDORI Nagano dining floor
places.note: Station restaurant floor with several Shinshu izakaya.

food.name: Shinshu miso dishes
food.desc: Nagano makes more miso than anywhere in Japan; it turns up in hot pots, ramen broth and even on grilled dumplings.

places.name: Shinanoji
places.note: Miso hot pot, handmade oyaki and rich miso soup; busy at lunch.

places.name: Ramen Misoya
places.note: Shinshu miso ramen and a hot dipping version.

places.name: Miso shops on Zenkoji Nakamise
places.note: Centuries-old brewers selling and sampling their own miso.

food.name: Shojin ryori
food.desc: The vegetarian temple cuisine of Zenkoji: sesame tofu, mountain vegetables and clear broths, served in the temple lodgings.

places.name: Fuchinobo shukubo
places.note: Temple lodging serving shojin ryori sets; book ahead.

places.name: Zenkoji shukubo along Omotesando
places.note: Around 39 temple lodgings, many open to non-staying diners.

places.name: Yayoiza
places.note: Historic restaurant near the temple with vegetarian Shinshu sets.

food.name: Shinshu apples and walnut sweets
food.desc: Nagano is Japan's apple country; look for apple pies, dried rings and kurumi walnut confections around the temple.

places.name: Nakamise-dori sweet shops
places.note: Rows of shops selling apple and walnut sweets, most with samples.

places.name: MIDORI Nagano
places.note: Station food hall stocking Shinshu apple products and gifts.

places.name: Roadside fruit stands on the Apple Line
places.note: Orchard stalls selling fruit straight from the trees in autumn.

food.name: Nagano sake
food.desc: Shinshu has more sake breweries than almost any other prefecture, fed by Japan Alps snowmelt; try a crisp local junmai.

places.name: Sake tasting bars on Zenkoji Omotesando
places.note: Several small bars pour flights of Nagano-only breweries.

places.name: Gondo shopping arcade izakaya
places.note: Deep local sake lists to go with basashi and grilled dishes.

places.name: MIDORI Nagano Shinshu sake corner
places.note: One-stop selection of prefecture breweries for tasting or gifts.

food.name: Amazake
food.desc: Thick, barely alcoholic fermented rice drink served steaming hot - the classic thing to hold on a cold Zenkoji morning.

places.name: Nakamise-dori tea houses
places.note: Hot amazake sold from the shops along the temple approach.

places.name: Ogawa no Sho
places.note: Serves amazake alongside its hearth-grilled oyaki.

places.name: Zenkoji Omotesando cafes
places.note: Traditional cafes doing amazake and matcha through winter.

landmarks: Zenkō-ji Temple
Japan's revered 7th-century temple guards its first Buddhist image; pilgrims descend into a pitch-black tunnel below the altar seeking the 'key to paradise'.
Jigokudani Snow Monkey Park
Wild Japanese macaques soak blissfully in steaming hot-spring pools amid winter snows, a world-famous spectacle in the Yokoyu River valley.
Togakushi Shrine
Five ancient shrines climb a sacred mountain of ninja legend, reached by a spine-tingling avenue of 400-year-old towering cedars.
Nakamise-dōri (Zenkō-ji Omotesandō)
The stone-paved pilgrimage approach to Zenkō-ji brims with temple lodgings, soba restaurants, sake shops, and oyaki dumpling vendors.
Matsushiro Castle Town
The Sanada clan's former fief preserves castle gates, samurai residences, and a clan school, an atmospheric Edo-period pocket south of the city.
Kawanakajima Battlefield (Hachimanbara)
Statues of dueling warlords Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin commemorate five legendary 16th-century battles fought on this riverside plain.
Togakushi Ninja Museum and Ninpo Center
At the home of the Togakure ninja school, trick houses, shuriken throwing, and artifacts bring the mountain's covert history to life.
Obuse
This chestnut-sweets town nearby cherishes the Hokusai-kan museum of the master's late works and the painted ceiling he left at Ganshō-in temple.
M-Wave (Nagano Olympic Museum)
The elegant wooden-roofed speed-skating arena of the 1998 Winter Games houses a museum of Olympic memorabilia and public ice sessions.
Yudanaka and Shibu Onsen
Atmospheric hot-spring towns of cobbled lanes and nine public bathhouses, where yukata-clad guests stroll en route to the snow monkeys.

train.note: Japan has no international trains. The Hokuriku Shinkansen reaches Nagano from Tokyo in 80 to 110 minutes depending on whether you catch a fast Kagayaki or a stopping Hakutaka, with a base fare around Y8,200, and continues west to Toyama and Kanazawa. From Nagoya the Shinano limited express runs hourly in about 3 hours for Y7,330, and from Osaka or Kyoto you go either via Nagoya or via Kanazawa, roughly 4 to 4.5 hours either way and covered by the Japan Rail Pass. The private Nagano Dentetsu line runs from beneath Nagano Station to Obuse and Yudanaka for the snow monkeys, and Shinano Railway covers the old JR line toward Karuizawa.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Japan. Highway coaches from Tokyo leave the Shinjuku terminal and the Sunshine City Prince Hotel in Ikebukuro, taking about 3 hours 30 minutes for Y4,000 one way or Y7,200 return. Hankyu and Nankai run services from Osaka (about Y6,200) and Kyoto (about Y5,300), taking 7 to 9 hours depending on whether you travel by day or overnight. Alpico Kotsu (https://www.alpico.co.jp/) handles regional coaches to Matsumoto and Hakuba, and Nagaden Bus (https://www.nagaden-net.co.jp/) runs the express to the Snow Monkey Park at Kanbayashi Onsen.

ferry.note: Nagano is deep in the mountains of central Honshu with no coastline, so there are no ferry or passenger boat services.

half.name: Matsumoto Castle
half.blurb: One of Japan's oldest original wooden castles, its black-walled keep earning it the nickname Crow Castle.

half.name: Hakuba Valley
half.blurb: An alpine valley at the base of the Northern Japan Alps, a ski resort area that turns green and hikeable in summer.

full.name: Kamikochi
full.blurb: A car-free alpine valley in Chubu-Sangaku National Park, with the Azusa River running beneath the Hotaka mountain range.

full.name: Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route
full.blurb: A mountain transport route of cable cars, ropeways, and buses crossing the Northern Alps, famous for its towering spring snow walls.
